sentences.text: Goronyosaurus was a small mosasaur that measured up to 5.14 meters in length.
Researcher Soliar derived this body length estimate of 5.14 meters from a skull length of 0.71 meters.
The premaxillae bear strong teeth, with the frontmost tooth positioned directly behind the start of the snout.
The maxillae bones are unusual for mosasaurids because they bear teeth that extend behind the front of the eye socket.
There are probably around eleven teeth in the maxilla, though the exact number is uncertain due to breakage.
Multiple dorsal vertebrae are known, with centra that begin cylindrical but become flattened near the pelvis.
Zygapophyses are weakly present in dorsal vertebrae, unlike in the cervical vertebrae, but inter-arch articulations are absent in both.
Goronyosaurus possesses teeth that are unlike those of any other mosasaur.
The skull and teeth resemble crocodiles, featuring ten elongated canine-like teeth that interlocked with holes in the opposite jaw.
Nerve traces in its snout suggest the animal relied more on touch and smell than sight.
The genus Goronyosaurus was established by Azzaroli and colleagues in 1972.
The species Goronyosaurus nigeriensis was originally described by Swinton and others in 1930.
The type specimen was initially named Mosasaurus nigeriensis in 1930 before being moved to its own genus.
Unique anatomical adaptations found in later fossils led to the reclassification of the species into the new genus Goronyosaurus in 1972.
The original type specimen, consisting of two vertebrae, was noted by Franz von Nopcsa in 1925 in northwestern Nigeria.
The remains were described more completely by Swinton and colleagues in 1930.
William Swinton described the species as Mosasaurus nigeriensis in 1930 based on jaw fossils from Maastrichtian deposits.
Goronyosaurus had relatively longer jaws than other mosasaurs, with jaw muscles positioned further back to allow for a rapid bite.
Studies indicate Goronyosaurus teeth were better adapted for cutting meat than piercing bones.
Unlike most mosasaurs with cutting teeth, Goronyosaurus had straight teeth with rounded apices designed for smashing food.
Goronyosaurus likely inhabited turbid waters like estuaries and fed on large fish and other marine reptiles.
Goronyosaurus specialized in a crocodile-like skull with an elongated rigid build and interlocking teeth, suited for hunting in murky settings.
Goronyosaurus was originally classified in its own subfamily, Goronyosaurinae, but this classification was later found to be incorrect.
In 1988, Lingham-Soliar placed Goronyosaurus within the subfamily Tylosaurinae based on cranial characteristics.
A 2010 analysis suggested Goronyosaurus belongs in Mosasaurinae because it forms a clade with Prognathodon, Plesiotylosaurus, and Ectenosaurus.
Strong et al. assigned Goronyosaurus to the subfamily Plioplatecarpinae in 2020.
Fossils of Goronyosaurus are exclusively known from the Late Maastrichtian period in West Africa.
Fossils have been found in the Dukamaje Formation of Niger and Nigeria and the Farin Doutchi Formation of Niger.
All known Goronyosaurus fossils come from the Dukamaje and Farin Doutchi Formations in Niger and Nigeria, located within the Iullemmeden Basin.
Goronyosaurus lived during the Maastrichtian stage, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
Azzaroli and colleagues proposed in 1972 that Goronyosaurus had an extremely long and tall jugal bone, a view later disputed.
Soliar disregarded Azzaroli's functional implications for the jugal bone in 1988 due to a lack of precedent for such an adaptation.
Halstead and Middleton doubted the identity of the jugal bones in 1982, leading Soliar to propose in 1988 that the structure was a taphonomic mix of the jugal and mandible.
Lingham-Soliar (1999) suggested Goronyosaurus represented an early stage of adaptation to freshwater rivers, a transition that was likely prevented by the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction.
